details:
**Waiting for Godot**
Beckett's most famous play and a landmark of the Theatre of the Absurd. Two tramps, Vladimir (Didi) and Estragon (Gogo), wait on a country road by a lone tree for a man named Godot, who never arrives. Both acts end with the line "Let's go" followed by the stage direction "They do not move."

**Vladimir and Estragon**
The two tramps of Waiting for Godot, who pass the time with bickering, routines such as swapping bowler hats, and repeated talk of hanging themselves from the tree. Vladimir discusses why only one of the four Gospels mentions that one of the two thieves crucified with Jesus was saved, and he sings a round about a dog that steals a crust of bread. Estragon dreams of wandering in the Pyrenees and rejects the turnip and radish Vladimir offers him because he wants a carrot.

**Pozzo and Lucky**
The master and slave who pass through Waiting for Godot. Pozzo drives Lucky on a rope, and Lucky dances a dance called "The Net" and kicks Estragon in the shin. In Act II, Pozzo has gone blind and Lucky has gone mute, and the two are often read as reversing or blurring the roles of master and slave.

**Lucky's "Think!" monologue**
When Pozzo orders him to "Think!", Lucky delivers a long, unpunctuated speech of academic gibberish about a "personal God quaquaquaqua." It cites the "public works of Puncher and Wattman" and the "Acacacacademy of Anthropopopometry."

**The tree and the boy**
The only scenery in Waiting for Godot is a bare tree, which sprouts a few leaves in Act II as the only sign that time has passed. At the end of each act, a boy arrives to say that Godot will not come today but surely tomorrow. The boy tends Godot's goats, and he reports that Godot beats his brother, who tends the sheep.

**Susan Sontag's Sarajevo production**
In 1993, during the Siege of Sarajevo, Susan Sontag directed a candlelit production of Waiting for Godot in the besieged city.

**Endgame**
Beckett's one-act play set in a bare room with two small windows in an apparently post-apocalyptic world. Its central characters are the blind Hamm, who cannot stand and sits in a wheelchair, and his servant Clov, who cannot sit. Clov opens the play with "Finished, it's finished, nearly finished," and Hamm repeats "Me to play" like a chess player. At the end, Hamm covers his face with his bloodstained handkerchief.

**Nagg and Nell in the trash cans**
Hamm's legless parents in Endgame live in two ashbins (trash cans) and try but fail to kiss. They lost their legs ("shanks") in a tandem bicycle accident in the Ardennes. Hamm also asks to be wheeled around the walls of the room and put back exactly in its center, and he has a three-legged black toy dog, which Clov hits him with near the end.

**Krapp's Last Tape**
A one-act play in which the old Krapp, on his 69th birthday, eats bananas and listens to a tape recording he made at 39. He savors the word "spool," laughs at his younger self, and finally records one last tape.

**Happy Days**
A play in which Winnie is buried up to her waist in Act I and up to her neck in Act II in a mound of earth. She chatters cheerfully, rummages in her handbag (which holds a revolver), watches an ant and laughs at the word "formication," and remarks on "the way man adapts himself to changing conditions." Her husband Willie mostly stays out of sight and reads aloud from a newspaper.

**Not I**
A short play in which the only lit part of the stage is a woman's disembodied Mouth speaking rapidly about her life ("back in the field"). A silent, hooded Auditor stands nearby.

**The Trilogy: Molloy, Malone Dies, The Unnamable**
Beckett's three postwar novels, which he first wrote in French. In Molloy, the detective Jacques Moran is sent to track down the title wanderer. In Malone Dies, a bedridden man who is unsure whether he is in a hospital or an asylum tells stories about a character called Sapo, later renamed Macmann. In The Unnamable, a disembodied voice thinks about invented figures such as Mahood and Worm.

**Late short plays: Footfalls, Rockaby, A Piece of Monologue**
Footfalls shows May pacing while she speaks with the voice of her (possibly dead) mother. In Rockaby, a woman sits in a rocking chair listening to her own recorded voice. A Piece of Monologue is an old man's brief meditation on birth and death.

**Biography: Irish, Paris, and the Resistance**
Beckett was born in Dublin and studied at Trinity College. He settled in Paris in 1937, worked for the French Resistance during World War II, and later hid in rural France doing farm work. He wrote many of his works in French, and he won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1969.
